nodes.label: Measuring economic growth: GDP and GDP per capita
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand how GDP and GDP per capita are constructed and used to compare economies over time and space.
essentialPoints: GDP measures total output/income of an economy
GDP per capita divides by population to allow comparison of living standards
Historical GDP estimates rely on reconstructed/incomplete data
Real vs nominal adjustments needed for cross-time comparison
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Introduction and Pre-Modern Growth: pre-1500

nodes.label: Measurement challenges in historical national accounts
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Recognise the limitations and biases in reconstructing historical income/output data.
essentialPoints: Sparse pre-modern records force estimation from proxies (wages, prices, tax records)
Purchasing power parity adjustments needed for cross-country comparison
Estimates carry wide margins of error, especially further back in time
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Introduction and Pre-Modern Growth: pre-1500

nodes.label: Malthusian model of pre-modern economies
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the Malthusian mechanism linking population, resources, and living standards before modern growth.
essentialPoints: Population growth is positively linked to income/living standards via fertility and mortality
Fixed land/resources mean diminishing returns to labour as population rises
Income above subsistence raises population, which then pulls income back toward subsistence
Technology gains raise population size in the long run rather than sustained per-capita income
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Introduction and Pre-Modern Growth: pre-1500

nodes.label: Evidence and critique of the Malthusian trap
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Evaluate how well the Malthusian model fits historical evidence and its limitations.
essentialPoints: Long-run stagnant per-capita incomes pre-1500 broadly consistent with Malthusian prediction
Some regions show episodes of rising living standards not fully explained (e.g. post-Black Death Europe)
Model struggles to explain the eventual escape into sustained modern growth
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Introduction and Pre-Modern Growth: pre-1500

nodes.label: Technological change and agricultural productivity pre-1500
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the role of slow technological progress in pre-modern economies.
essentialPoints: Agricultural innovation (crop rotation, tools) raised output but slowly
Diffusion of technology was limited by trade and communication constraints
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Introduction and Pre-Modern Growth: pre-1500

nodes.label: The 'Great Divergence' question: why Europe?
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Frame the central historiographical question of why sustained growth first emerged in Western Europe rather than Asia.
essentialPoints: Pre-1500 income levels across Eurasia were broadly comparable
By 1800-1900 a large gap opened between Western Europe and the rest of the world
Explaining the timing and cause of this divergence is a central debate

nodes.label: Institutional explanations for economic development (property rights, constraints on rulers)
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand how secure property rights and checks on rulers are argued to promote investment and growth.
essentialPoints: Secure property rights encourage investment by reducing expropriation risk
Institutions limiting arbitrary rule (e.g. parliamentary constraint) associated with commercial development
Institutional quality varied across early modern European states

nodes.label: Case study: England's Glorious Revolution (1688) and credible commitment
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Use the 1688 settlement as an applied test of institutional theories of growth.
essentialPoints: 1688 constrained monarchical power via Parliament
Argued to have improved credibility of government debt repayment and property rights
Debate over whether institutional change actually preceded or followed economic growth

nodes.label: Atlantic trade and colonial expansion
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the growth of Atlantic trade networks and their economic significance.
essentialPoints: European expansion opened new trade routes and colonial resource extraction
Atlantic trading nations (Britain, Netherlands) grew disproportionately relative to landlocked/Mediterranean states
Trade profits linked to urban growth and merchant capital accumulation

nodes.label: Atlantic trade as a driver of institutional change
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the argument linking merchant wealth from Atlantic trade to demands for political constraints on rulers.
essentialPoints: Profits from Atlantic trade empowered merchant classes
Merchant classes lobbied for institutions protecting their commercial interests
This link is proposed to explain why Atlantic-facing nations developed stronger constraining institutions

nodes.label: Geographic explanations for divergence (resources, disease, climate)
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand geography-based explanations of comparative development.
essentialPoints: Access to coal and other resources argued to matter for later industrialisation
Disease environment affected settlement patterns and colonial institution choices
Climate and geography shape agricultural productivity and trade access

nodes.label: Cultural/ideational explanations for divergence (values, religion, science)
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand arguments linking cultural or ideational change (e.g. Protestant ethic, scientific revolution) to economic development.
essentialPoints: Weberian argument links Protestant work ethic to capitalist development
Scientific revolution argued to foster a culture of experimentation applicable to production
Cultural explanations are contested versus institutional/geographic accounts

nodes.label: Evaluating institutional vs geographic vs cultural explanations of divergence
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Weigh competing explanations for the Great Divergence against evidence.
essentialPoints: Institutional theory struggles to explain timing precisely (institutions changed decades before takeoff)
Geographic theory struggles to explain why coal became valuable only once demand from industrialisation existed
Cultural theories face difficulty in being tested rigorously against alternatives
Most historians now favour multi-causal accounts combining institutions, geography, and trade

nodes.label: Defining the British Industrial Revolution
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand what is meant by the Industrial Revolution as a historical and economic phenomenon.
essentialPoints: Period c.1750-1850 marked by mechanisation, factory production, and sustained productivity growth
First historical instance of escape from Malthusian stagnation
Characterised by structural shift from agriculture to industry
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The British Industrial Revolution: 1750-1850

nodes.label: Key technological innovations of the Industrial Revolution
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Identify the major technologies driving industrial transformation.
essentialPoints: Steam engine enabled mechanised power independent of water/wind location
Textile innovations (spinning jenny, power loom) mechanised manufacturing
Innovations clustered in specific sectors (textiles, iron, coal) before spreading
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The British Industrial Revolution: 1750-1850

nodes.label: Explanations for why the Industrial Revolution began in Britain
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the leading theories of British industrial primacy.
essentialPoints: High-wage economy incentivised labour-saving mechanisation (Allen's high-wage hypothesis)
Cheap and accessible coal reduced energy costs for mechanised production
Institutional and financial development (patent system, capital markets) supported innovation
Colonial and trade wealth provided capital and markets
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The British Industrial Revolution: 1750-1850

nodes.label: Evaluating the high-wage/cheap-coal hypothesis for British industrialisation
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Assess the strength of Allen's high-wage hypothesis as an explanation.
essentialPoints: High wages made labour-saving machinery profitable specifically in Britain relative to competitors
Critics argue wage/price ratios were not uniquely favourable enough to fully explain timing
Coal proximity reduced the cost disadvantage of early inefficient steam engines
Alternative accounts stress human capital and scientific culture instead
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The British Industrial Revolution: 1750-1850

nodes.label: The rise of the factory system
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand how production organisation shifted from domestic/cottage industry to factories.
essentialPoints: Factories concentrated workers and machinery to exploit economies of scale and power sources
Shift undermined the domestic (putting-out) system of production
Enabled closer supervision and division of labour within firms
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The British Industrial Revolution: 1750-1850

nodes.label: Structural change: sectoral shift from agriculture to industry
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the reallocation of labour and output across sectors during industrialisation.
essentialPoints: Share of workforce in agriculture fell as industrial and service sectors grew
Urbanisation accompanied the sectoral shift as workers moved to factory towns
Productivity growth in agriculture released labour for industry
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The British Industrial Revolution: 1750-1850

nodes.label: The standard-of-living debate: optimists vs pessimists
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the historiographical debate on whether industrialisation raised or lowered working-class living standards.
essentialPoints: Pessimists argue real wages stagnated or fell during early industrialisation despite rising output
Optimists argue real wage evidence shows eventual gains, especially post-1830s/40s
Debate hinges on choice of price index, wage series, and time period examined

nodes.label: Constructing historical real wage indices
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand how nominal wage and price data are combined into real wage series.
essentialPoints: Real wages calculated by deflating nominal wages by a cost-of-living index
Choice of consumption basket (goods included) significantly affects results
Regional and occupational wage variation complicates national aggregates

nodes.label: Biological standard of living: height and mortality evidence
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the use of anthropometric and mortality data as alternative living standards measures.
essentialPoints: Average height reflects net nutritional status during childhood/adolescence
Height and life expectancy series sometimes show decline even where wage data show stagnation/growth
Urbanisation associated with worsened disease environment ('urban penalty')

nodes.label: Inequality during early industrialisation
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand how the gains from industrialisation were distributed.
essentialPoints: Capital owners and skilled workers captured disproportionate early gains
Kuznets-curve-style argument: inequality rises then falls over industrialisation process
Unskilled/child labour faced poor conditions despite aggregate output growth

nodes.label: The 'first globalisation' 1870-1914: trade, capital, and labour flows
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Characterise the scale and drivers of pre-WWI globalisation.
essentialPoints: Falling transport costs (steamships, railways) integrated global commodity markets
Mass migration flows (e.g. Europe to Americas) integrated labour markets
International capital flows (British foreign investment) financed global infrastructure

nodes.label: The classical gold standard
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the mechanics and role of the gold standard in pre-WWI globalisation.
essentialPoints: Currencies fixed their value in terms of gold, fixing exchange rates between countries
Balance-of-payments adjustment theoretically operated via gold flows and price-specie-flow mechanism
Provided credibility for international lending and trade
System required countries to subordinate domestic monetary policy to gold convertibility

nodes.label: Convergence and divergence among nations 1870-1914
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand which economies converged toward the industrial leaders and which fell further behind.
essentialPoints: Migration and capital flows facilitated wage/income convergence among Atlantic-economy participants
Regions without access to trade/migration networks (e.g. parts of Asia, Africa) diverged further
Convergence was conditional on openness and factor mobility, not automatic

nodes.label: The Second Industrial Revolution: new technologies and followers
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the technological wave that allowed the US and Germany to catch up with and overtake Britain.
essentialPoints: New technologies: electricity, chemicals, steel, internal combustion engine
US and Germany invested heavily in science-based industries and education
Britain's early-mover advantage became a relative disadvantage due to sunk capital in old technologies

nodes.label: Trade policy reactions: tariffs and the backlash against globalisation
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand rising protectionism as a political response to the first globalisation.
essentialPoints: Grain invasion from the Americas hurt European agricultural interests, prompting tariffs
Political coalitions of threatened domestic producers lobbied for protection
Some countries (e.g. Britain) retained free trade while others (e.g. Germany, France) protected

nodes.label: WWI as an economic shock: disruption of trade and finance
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand how WWI disrupted the pre-war global economic order.
essentialPoints: War suspended gold convertibility and disrupted international trade flows
Massive government debts and reparations reshaped international financial relations
Human and physical capital destruction reduced productive capacity in combatant nations

nodes.label: Interwar restoration of the gold standard and its problems
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand attempts to rebuild the gold standard after WWI and why they failed.
essentialPoints: Countries returned to gold often at pre-war (overvalued) parities, e.g. Britain 1925
Overvaluation caused deflationary pressure and unemployment in adjusting economies
Rigid gold constraint limited ability of central banks to respond to shocks

nodes.label: Causes of the Great Depression
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the leading explanations for the onset and severity of the 1929-1933 downturn.
essentialPoints: 1929 US stock market crash reduced wealth and consumer/investor confidence
Gold standard constraints transmitted deflationary shocks internationally
Banking crises and monetary contraction (per Friedman-Schwartz) deepened the downturn
Protectionist responses (e.g. Smoot-Hawley tariff) reduced international trade further

nodes.label: The gold standard as a transmission mechanism and constraint on recovery
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand Eichengreen's argument linking gold standard adherence to depression severity and recovery timing.
essentialPoints: Countries that left gold earlier recovered sooner (freed to pursue expansionary monetary policy)
Adherence to gold constrained central banks from cutting interest rates or expanding money supply
Cross-country evidence on exit timing supports gold standard as a key depression propagator

nodes.label: Interwar deglobalisation: collapse of trade and capital flows
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the reversal of pre-1914 globalisation trends during the interwar period.
essentialPoints: Global trade volumes and capital flows fell sharply relative to pre-WWI peak
Protectionism and capital controls proliferated across major economies
Migration restrictions tightened, reversing pre-war labour mobility

nodes.label: WWII economic mobilisation and production
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand how major economies organised production for total war.
essentialPoints: Governments directed resources via planning, rationing, and controlled prices
US industrial capacity mobilised rapidly, becoming the 'arsenal of democracy'
War production ended interwar unemployment in combatant economies
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: War, Recovery, and Decolonisation: 1939-1961

nodes.label: The Bretton Woods system
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the postwar international monetary architecture and its institutions.
essentialPoints: Fixed but adjustable exchange rates pegged to the US dollar, which was convertible to gold
Created the IMF (balance-of-payments support) and World Bank (development finance)
Aimed to combine exchange rate stability with domestic policy autonomy ('embedded liberalism')
Capital controls permitted to protect fixed exchange rates from speculative flows
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: War, Recovery, and Decolonisation: 1939-1961

nodes.label: The Marshall Plan and postwar European reconstruction
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the scale and role of US aid in postwar European recovery.
essentialPoints: US financed large-scale aid to Western Europe 1948-1952
Aimed to rebuild productive capacity and prevent the spread of communism
Debate over how much aid versus domestic institutional reform drove the 'Golden Age' recovery
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: War, Recovery, and Decolonisation: 1939-1961

nodes.label: The postwar 'Golden Age' of growth (1950s-1970s)
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Characterise the exceptional growth performance of advanced economies after WWII.
essentialPoints: Western Europe and Japan grew rapidly, partly via catch-up/convergence to US productivity levels
High investment rates and technology transfer supported rapid capital deepening
Stable macroeconomic and international monetary environment (Bretton Woods) supported growth
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: War, Recovery, and Decolonisation: 1939-1961

nodes.label: Decolonisation and its economic consequences
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the process and economic legacy of decolonisation in the postwar period.
essentialPoints: Former colonies gained political independence across Africa and Asia post-1945
New states inherited institutions and infrastructure shaped by colonial extraction priorities
Economic performance post-independence varied widely, feeding debates on colonial legacy effects
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: War, Recovery, and Decolonisation: 1939-1961

nodes.label: Debating the long-run economic legacy of colonialism
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Evaluate arguments on how colonial institutions shaped post-independence development.
essentialPoints: Extractive colonial institutions argued to persist and hinder post-independence growth (Acemoglu-Robinson style argument)
Settler mortality/colonisation strategy argued to explain variation in institutional quality left behind
Critics highlight difficulty isolating colonial effects from geography and pre-colonial conditions
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: War, Recovery, and Decolonisation: 1939-1961

nodes.label: Import substitution industrialisation (ISI)
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the ISI development strategy adopted by many postcolonial and Latin American economies.
essentialPoints: Strategy of protecting domestic industry via tariffs/quotas to replace imports with domestic production
Aimed to build industrial base and reduce dependence on primary commodity exports
Often led to inefficient, uncompetitive industries reliant on continued protection
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Planning, Divergence, and Inflation: 1961-1979

nodes.label: Central planning in socialist/communist economies
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the mechanics and performance of centrally planned economies.
essentialPoints: State ownership and central allocation replaced market price signals for production decisions
Achieved rapid initial industrialisation via forced resource mobilisation (e.g. USSR)
Suffered from information and incentive problems, leading to eventual stagnation
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Planning, Divergence, and Inflation: 1961-1979

nodes.label: East Asian export-led growth ('miracle' economies)
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the alternative export-oriented development strategy pursued by East Asian economies.
essentialPoints: Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, etc. pursued export-oriented rather than import-substituting industrialisation
Combined state industrial policy with strong investment in education and high savings/investment rates
Achieved sustained rapid catch-up growth, contrasting with ISI performance elsewhere
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Planning, Divergence, and Inflation: 1961-1979

nodes.label: Evaluating import substitution vs export-led growth strategies
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Compare the outcomes of ISI and export-led strategies across developing regions.
essentialPoints: Export-led East Asian economies achieved faster and more sustained growth than most ISI economies
ISI protected industries often failed to become internationally competitive, sustaining inefficiency
Differences partly attributed to macroeconomic discipline and openness rather than industrial policy alone
Debate remains over how much state intervention itself (vs external orientation) explains outcomes
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Planning, Divergence, and Inflation: 1961-1979

nodes.label: The collapse of Bretton Woods (1971-1973)
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand why the fixed exchange rate system broke down in the early 1970s.
essentialPoints: US inflation and rising external deficits undermined dollar-gold convertibility credibility
Nixon suspended dollar convertibility to gold in 1971 ('Nixon Shock')
Major currencies moved to floating exchange rates by 1973, ending the fixed-rate era
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Planning, Divergence, and Inflation: 1961-1979

nodes.label: Oil shocks and stagflation in the 1970s
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand how the 1973 and 1979 oil price shocks produced simultaneous inflation and stagnation.
essentialPoints: OPEC oil price increases raised costs across advanced economies, acting as a negative supply shock
Resulted in simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment ('stagflation'), challenging existing macroeconomic policy models
Ended the low-inflation, high-growth conditions of the Golden Age
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Planning, Divergence, and Inflation: 1961-1979

nodes.label: The Great Inflation of the 1970s
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the causes and policy debates around sustained high inflation in advanced economies during the 1970s.
essentialPoints: Loose monetary policy combined with supply shocks fuelled sustained inflation across advanced economies
Breakdown of fixed exchange rates removed an external discipline on monetary expansion
Policy responses were initially inconsistent, contributing to persistent inflation expectations
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: Planning, Divergence, and Inflation: 1961-1979

nodes.label: Market-oriented reforms: Thatcherism and Reaganomics
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the shift toward deregulation, privatisation, and monetarist policy in the UK and US.
essentialPoints: Privatisation of state-owned industries and deregulation of markets in the UK and US
Monetarist disinflation policy prioritised controlling money supply growth over full employment targets
Reduced trade union power and lowered top marginal tax rates

nodes.label: The 1980s Latin American debt crisis
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the causes and consequences of the sovereign debt crises in developing economies.
essentialPoints: Developing economies had borrowed heavily in the 1970s (partly recycled oil-exporter surpluses)
Rising US interest rates in early 1980s sharply raised debt-servicing costs
Multiple sovereign defaults/restructurings triggered a 'lost decade' of growth for Latin America

nodes.label: The Washington Consensus and structural adjustment
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the policy package promoted by international institutions for indebted developing economies.
essentialPoints: Package including fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation, privatisation, and deregulation
Promoted by IMF/World Bank conditionality attached to structural adjustment loans
Criticised for underestimating short-run social costs and institutional preconditions for reform success

nodes.label: Collapse of the Soviet bloc and transition economies
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the economic transition from planning to markets after 1989-1991.
essentialPoints: USSR and Eastern bloc transitioned from central planning toward market economies after 1989-91
'Shock therapy' rapid liberalisation approach contrasted with gradualist approaches (e.g. China)
Transition associated with severe short-run output collapse in many former Soviet states

nodes.label: China's post-1978 economic reforms
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand China's gradualist market reform trajectory and its growth consequences.
essentialPoints: Deng Xiaoping-era reforms introduced market incentives while retaining state control gradually
Special Economic Zones opened China to foreign investment and export-led growth
Sustained very high growth rates over subsequent decades, contrasting with Soviet shock therapy outcomes

nodes.label: Evaluating shock therapy vs gradualist transition strategies
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Compare the outcomes of rapid versus gradual transition from planned to market economies.
essentialPoints: China's gradualist approach delivered sustained high growth without major output collapse
Russia/Eastern Europe's rapid liberalisation associated with sharp short-run depressions
Differences may reflect initial conditions (agrarian vs industrial base) as much as policy choice itself
Debate over whether gradualism merely delayed necessary adjustment costs

nodes.label: The 'second globalisation' wave post-1980s
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the renewed expansion of trade and capital flows from the late 20th century.
essentialPoints: Trade liberalisation (GATT/WTO rounds) reduced tariffs across advanced and developing economies
Capital account liberalisation increased cross-border financial flows
Multinational firms built global supply chains, integrating developing-economy manufacturing

nodes.label: The 2008 Global Financial Crisis
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand the causes and international transmission of the 2008 crisis.
essentialPoints: US subprime mortgage lending and securitisation created fragile, interconnected financial exposures
Collapse of major financial institutions (e.g. Lehman Brothers) triggered global credit market freeze
Crisis transmitted internationally via trade collapse and financial contagion
Policy responses included large-scale monetary easing and fiscal stimulus/bank bailouts
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The Contemporary World Economy: 2001-present

nodes.label: China's rise as a global economic power
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand China's continued growth and integration into the world economy post-2001.
essentialPoints: WTO accession (2001) accelerated China's export-led integration into world trade
Sustained high growth made China the world's second-largest economy
Rising Chinese demand reshaped global commodity markets and manufacturing supply chains
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The Contemporary World Economy: 2001-present

nodes.label: Rising inequality and the political backlash against globalisation
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand contemporary debates on globalisation's distributional effects and resulting political responses.
essentialPoints: Trade and technology change linked to wage stagnation for some groups in advanced economies (e.g. 'China shock' literature)
Rising within-country inequality coexisted with falling global inequality via developing-economy catch-up
Political backlash manifested in protectionist and populist policy movements (e.g. Brexit, US tariffs)
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The Contemporary World Economy: 2001-present

nodes.label: Contemporary global economic challenges: climate, pandemic, geopolitics
nodes.theme: EC104: The World Economy: History and Theory
nodes.objective: Understand major ongoing challenges shaping the 21st-century world economy.
essentialPoints: Climate change poses long-run risks and requires costly mitigation/adaptation policy
COVID-19 pandemic caused a synchronised global supply and demand shock with long recovery effects
Rising geopolitical tension (e.g. US-China rivalry) is reshaping trade and supply chain patterns
specRefs: EC104 syllabus: The Contemporary World Economy: 2001-present

nodes.label: Circular flow of income
nodes.objective: Understand the basic circular flow of income between households, firms, government, and abroad
essentialPoints: Households supply factors of production to firms, firms pay income
Leakages: savings, taxes, imports; injections: investment, government spending, exports

nodes.label: GDP: definition and measurement
nodes.objective: Define GDP as total value of output produced in an economy over a period
essentialPoints: GDP = total market value of final goods and services produced within a country in a given period
Distinguishes final goods from intermediate goods to avoid double counting
specRefs: EC108 syllabus: National Accounts, Output, GDP

nodes.label: Value added and avoiding double counting
nodes.objective: Understand value added as the sum method of calculating GDP without double counting intermediate goods
essentialPoints: Value added = value of output minus value of intermediate inputs
Summing value added across all stages of production equals GDP

nodes.label: Three measures of GDP: output, income, expenditure
nodes.objective: Understand that GDP can be measured via output, income, or expenditure approaches and these are theoretically equivalent
essentialPoints: Output approach sums value added across sectors
Income approach sums factor incomes (wages, profits, rent)
Expenditure approach sums C+I+G+(X-M)

nodes.label: Nominal vs real GDP and GDP deflator
nodes.objective: Distinguish nominal GDP (current prices) from real GDP (constant prices) and use the GDP deflator to convert between them
essentialPoints: Nominal GDP measured at current prices, real GDP at constant base-year prices
GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP/Real GDP) x 100
Real GDP growth isolates changes in output from changes in prices

nodes.label: Limitations of GDP as a welfare measure
nodes.objective: Evaluate GDP's shortcomings as a measure of wellbeing
essentialPoints: Excludes non-market activity (household production, informal economy)
Ignores distribution of income across population
Ignores externalities such as environmental degradation
Does not capture leisure time or quality of life

nodes.label: Unemployment: definition and measurement
nodes.objective: Define unemployment and the labour force, and understand the unemployment rate calculation
essentialPoints: Unemployed: without work, available for work, actively seeking work
Labour force = employed + unemployed
Unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force

nodes.label: Types of unemployment: frictional, structural, cyclical
nodes.objective: Distinguish frictional, structural, and cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment as separate causes
essentialPoints: Frictional: short-term search/matching unemployment between jobs
Structural: mismatch of skills/location with available jobs, often persistent
Cyclical: arises from deficient aggregate demand during downturns

nodes.label: Natural rate of unemployment
nodes.objective: Understand the natural rate of unemployment as the rate consistent with stable inflation, comprising frictional and structural unemployment
essentialPoints: Natural rate = frictional + structural unemployment, excludes cyclical component
Economy at natural rate is at potential/full-employment output

nodes.label: Inflation: definition and price indices (CPI)
nodes.objective: Define inflation as a sustained rise in the general price level and understand how CPI is constructed
essentialPoints: Inflation = sustained increase in the general price level over time
CPI measured via a weighted basket of goods and services representative of typical consumption

nodes.label: Costs of inflation
nodes.objective: Identify the economic costs associated with inflation
essentialPoints: Menu costs: firms incur costs of repricing goods
Shoe-leather costs: costs of holding less cash and more frequent bank visits
Redistributive effects between creditors and debtors under unexpected inflation
Uncertainty discourages investment and long-term planning

nodes.label: Money: definition and functions
nodes.objective: Define money and its functions in the economy
essentialPoints: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Money supply measured via monetary aggregates (e.g. narrow vs broad money)

nodes.label: Demand for money
nodes.objective: Understand the motives for holding money and factors determining money demand
essentialPoints: Transactions motive, precautionary motive, speculative motive for holding money
Money demand negatively related to interest rate, positively related to income

nodes.label: Money market equilibrium and the LM relationship
nodes.objective: Determine the equilibrium interest rate where money demand equals money supply, and derive the LM relationship between income and interest rate
essentialPoints: Equilibrium interest rate equates money demand to fixed money supply
Higher income raises money demand, requiring higher interest rate to restore equilibrium (LM curve)

nodes.label: Money market diagram: constructing and reading equilibrium
nodes.objective: Construct and interpret the money supply-demand diagram to find equilibrium interest rate
essentialPoints: Vertical money supply curve, downward-sloping money demand curve against interest rate
Shifts in money supply or demand change equilibrium interest rate

nodes.label: Bond prices and interest rates: inverse relationship
nodes.objective: Understand why bond prices and interest rates move inversely
essentialPoints: Bond yield determined by fixed coupon payment relative to price paid
Higher bond price implies lower yield for a given coupon, and vice versa

nodes.label: Role of the central bank and monetary policy tools
nodes.objective: Understand the central bank's control of money supply/interest rates via policy tools
essentialPoints: Central bank sets policy interest rate and/or controls money supply
Tools include open market operations, reserve requirements, and (unconventional) quantitative easing

nodes.label: Keynesian consumption function
nodes.objective: Understand the Keynesian consumption function relating consumption to current disposable income
essentialPoints: C = a + bYd, where a is autonomous consumption and b is the marginal propensity to consume
MPC assumed constant and between 0 and 1, average propensity to consume falls as income rises

nodes.label: Marginal propensity to consume and save
nodes.objective: Define MPC and MPS and their relationship
essentialPoints: MPC = change in consumption / change in disposable income
MPS = change in saving / change in disposable income, and MPC + MPS = 1

nodes.label: The consumption puzzle: cross-section vs time-series evidence
nodes.objective: Understand the empirical puzzle that the Keynesian function fits cross-section/short-run data but not long-run time-series data (stable APC)
essentialPoints: Cross-section and short-run time series data show APC falling with income, consistent with Keynesian function
Long-run time series data show a roughly constant APC, inconsistent with simple Keynesian function

nodes.label: Permanent income hypothesis
nodes.objective: Understand Friedman's permanent income hypothesis distinguishing permanent from transitory income
essentialPoints: Consumption depends on permanent (long-run expected) income, not current income
Transitory income fluctuations are largely saved rather than consumed
Resolves the consumption puzzle by explaining stable long-run APC

nodes.label: Life-cycle hypothesis of consumption
nodes.objective: Understand Modigliani's life-cycle hypothesis where individuals smooth consumption over their lifetime based on lifetime resources
essentialPoints: Individuals plan consumption to smooth it across working life and retirement using saving and borrowing
Consumption depends on expected lifetime income/wealth, not just current income
Also resolves the consumption puzzle via aggregation across age cohorts

nodes.label: Intertemporal consumption choice and consumption smoothing
nodes.objective: Understand that rational consumers use saving/borrowing to smooth consumption in response to income fluctuations
essentialPoints: Consumers can borrow or save to shift consumption between periods
Optimal consumption choice arises from maximising utility subject to intertemporal budget constraint

nodes.label: Investment: definition and types
nodes.objective: Define investment as an addition to the capital stock, distinguishing fixed investment and inventory investment
essentialPoints: Investment = spending on new capital goods (fixed investment) or changes in inventories
Gross investment vs net investment (net of depreciation)

nodes.label: Marginal efficiency of capital / net present value approach to investment
nodes.objective: Understand how firms decide on investment by comparing expected returns to the cost of capital via NPV/MEC
essentialPoints: Firms invest in projects where expected discounted returns exceed the cost of the project
Marginal efficiency of capital equates discounted expected returns to cost of investment
Investment demand is inversely related to the interest rate

nodes.label: Investment demand curve and sensitivity to interest rates
nodes.objective: Understand the downward-sloping investment demand curve against the interest rate
essentialPoints: As interest rate falls, more investment projects become profitable, raising desired investment
Diagram shows investment on horizontal axis and interest rate on vertical axis with a downward slope

nodes.label: Accelerator theory of investment
nodes.objective: Understand the accelerator model linking investment to the rate of change of output
essentialPoints: Investment depends on the change in output/demand, not its level
Small changes in output growth can cause large swings in investment (accelerator effect)

nodes.label: Why investment is the most volatile component of aggregate demand
nodes.objective: Evaluate why investment fluctuates more than consumption
essentialPoints: Investment decisions depend on volatile expectations about future profitability
Accelerator effect amplifies small output changes into large investment swings
Irreversibility and uncertainty make investment sensitive to confidence shocks

nodes.label: Government spending and the government budget
nodes.objective: Understand government spending as a component of aggregate demand and the government budget balance
essentialPoints: Government spending (G) includes purchases of goods/services and transfer payments
Budget balance = taxes minus government spending; deficit when spending exceeds tax revenue

nodes.label: Types of taxation and their effect on disposable income
nodes.objective: Understand how taxes reduce disposable income and affect consumption via the consumption function
essentialPoints: Direct taxes on income reduce disposable income directly
Taxes can be lump-sum or proportional to income, affecting the slope of the consumption function differently

nodes.label: Public debt and deficit financing
nodes.objective: Understand how persistent deficits accumulate into public debt and the concept of debt sustainability
essentialPoints: Government deficit financed by borrowing (issuing bonds), accumulating as public debt
Debt-to-GDP ratio used to assess fiscal sustainability

nodes.label: Keynesian cross (45-degree) diagram: aggregate expenditure and equilibrium output
nodes.objective: Construct and use the Keynesian cross diagram to determine equilibrium income where planned expenditure equals output
essentialPoints: Aggregate expenditure line = C + I + G + (X-M) plotted against income
Equilibrium output where the expenditure line intersects the 45-degree line (Y = AE)

nodes.label: The multiplier: derivation and formula
nodes.objective: Derive the government spending multiplier from the equilibrium condition and MPC
essentialPoints: An increase in autonomous spending raises income by more than the initial increase, via successive rounds of spending
Simple multiplier = 1/(1-MPC) in a closed economy with no taxes
Multiplier reduced by taxes and imports leaking out of the spending stream

nodes.label: Fiscal policy: definition and tools
nodes.objective: Define fiscal policy as the use of government spending and taxation to influence aggregate demand
essentialPoints: Fiscal policy involves changing G and/or taxes to influence the economy
Expansionary fiscal policy raises G or cuts taxes; contractionary does the reverse

nodes.label: Reasons for using fiscal policy to manage demand
nodes.objective: Understand the motivation for fiscal intervention: closing output gaps and stabilising the economy
essentialPoints: Aggregate demand can fall short of potential output, creating unemployment (recessionary gap)
Government can use fiscal policy to close output gaps and stabilise fluctuations

nodes.label: Advantages of fiscal policy
nodes.objective: Evaluate the benefits of fiscal policy as a demand management tool
essentialPoints: Directly and immediately increases aggregate demand via government purchases
Can be targeted at specific sectors or groups in need
Multiplier effect amplifies the initial impact on output

nodes.label: Disadvantages of fiscal policy
nodes.objective: Evaluate the drawbacks and limitations of fiscal policy
essentialPoints: Implementation and recognition lags mean policy may act too slowly to be effective
Crowding out: government borrowing may raise interest rates and reduce private investment
Increases public debt, raising future sustainability concerns
Subject to political constraints and time inconsistency

nodes.label: Crowding-out mechanism: government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment
nodes.objective: Trace the mechanism by which expansionary fiscal policy financed by borrowing can reduce private investment
essentialPoints: Government borrows to finance deficit, increasing demand for loanable funds
Increased borrowing raises interest rates in the money/bond market
Higher interest rates reduce private investment, offsetting some of the initial demand boost

nodes.label: Monetary policy: definition and transmission tools
nodes.objective: Define monetary policy as central bank actions to influence money supply and interest rates to affect demand
essentialPoints: Monetary policy changes interest rates or money supply to influence aggregate demand
Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates to stimulate borrowing and spending

nodes.label: Monetary policy transmission mechanism
nodes.objective: Trace the causal chain from a change in interest rates to a change in aggregate demand
essentialPoints: Central bank changes policy interest rate
Change in interest rate affects cost of borrowing, saving incentives, and asset prices
Changes in borrowing/saving and asset prices alter consumption and investment spending
Change in C and I feeds through the multiplier to change equilibrium output

nodes.label: Advantages of monetary policy
nodes.objective: Evaluate the benefits of monetary policy as a demand management tool
essentialPoints: Can be adjusted quickly and frequently compared to fiscal policy
Operationally independent central banks reduce political interference/time inconsistency
Does not directly add to government debt

nodes.label: Disadvantages of monetary policy
nodes.objective: Evaluate the limitations of monetary policy
essentialPoints: Long and variable transmission lags before effects are felt
Ineffective at the zero lower bound on interest rates
Effectiveness depends on interest-sensitivity of investment and consumption, which may be weak
Cannot target specific sectors or regions as precisely as fiscal policy

nodes.label: Aggregate demand curve: construction
nodes.objective: Derive the downward-sloping aggregate demand curve relating price level to equilibrium output
essentialPoints: Higher price level reduces real money balances, raising interest rates and reducing spending (via money market and Keynesian cross)
AD curve plots equilibrium output against price level, downward sloping

nodes.label: Shifts in the aggregate demand curve
nodes.objective: Understand how fiscal and monetary policy, and other autonomous demand changes, shift the AD curve
essentialPoints: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy shifts AD rightward
Changes in autonomous consumption, investment, or net exports also shift AD

nodes.label: Aggregate supply curve: short-run and long-run
nodes.objective: Distinguish the upward-sloping short-run aggregate supply curve from the vertical long-run aggregate supply curve at potential output
essentialPoints: Short-run AS slopes upward as sticky wages/prices mean higher prices raise firm output incentives
Long-run AS is vertical at potential output, determined by factors of production and technology, independent of price level

nodes.label: AD-AS equilibrium and adjustment to shocks
nodes.objective: Use the AD-AS model to determine short-run and long-run equilibrium price level and output following demand shocks
essentialPoints: Short-run equilibrium at intersection of AD and short-run AS
A demand shock moves output and prices in the short run but the economy adjusts back to potential output in the long run via wage/price adjustment

nodes.label: Original (short-run) Phillips curve: trade-off between inflation and unemployment
nodes.objective: Understand the empirical negative relationship observed between unemployment and inflation (wage inflation)
essentialPoints: Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between unemployment and (wage/price) inflation
Interpreted as a policy trade-off: lower unemployment achievable at the cost of higher inflation

nodes.label: Breakdown of the Phillips curve: stagflation of the 1970s
nodes.objective: Understand the empirical breakdown of the simple Phillips curve relationship during periods of simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment
essentialPoints: 1970s oil price shocks caused simultaneous rising inflation and rising unemployment (stagflation)
This contradicted the stable trade-off implied by the original Phillips curve

nodes.label: Expectations-augmented Phillips curve
nodes.objective: Understand how incorporating expected inflation resolves the breakdown of the simple Phillips curve
essentialPoints: Inflation depends on unemployment gap plus expected inflation: pi = pi^e - a(u - u*)
Shifts in expected inflation shift the short-run Phillips curve, explaining stagflation

nodes.label: Adaptive expectations of inflation
nodes.objective: Understand adaptive expectations as expectations formed by extrapolating from past inflation
essentialPoints: Expected inflation set equal to (or based on) past observed inflation
Expectations adjust gradually as actual inflation is observed

nodes.label: Long-run Phillips curve: vertical at the natural rate
nodes.objective: Understand that in the long run there is no trade-off, and the Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment
essentialPoints: Once expectations fully adjust, unemployment returns to the natural rate regardless of inflation
Long-run Phillips curve is vertical at u*, implying no permanent trade-off between inflation and unemployment

nodes.label: NAIRU: non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment
nodes.objective: Understand NAIRU as the unemployment rate consistent with stable (non-accelerating) inflation
essentialPoints: NAIRU is the unemployment rate at which actual inflation equals expected inflation
Unemployment below NAIRU causes accelerating inflation, above it causes decelerating inflation

nodes.label: Exchange rates: definition and nominal vs real
nodes.objective: Define the nominal exchange rate and the real exchange rate adjusting for relative price levels
essentialPoints: Nominal exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another
Real exchange rate = nominal exchange rate adjusted by relative price levels between countries

nodes.label: The foreign exchange market and exchange rate determination
nodes.objective: Understand how supply and demand for currency determine the exchange rate in the forex market
essentialPoints: Demand for a currency arises from exports, capital inflows, and demand for domestic assets
Exchange rate determined by equilibrium in the market for foreign exchange

nodes.label: Floating exchange rate regime
nodes.objective: Define a floating exchange rate as one determined freely by market forces of supply and demand
essentialPoints: Exchange rate adjusts continuously to equate supply and demand for the currency
No direct government/central bank intervention to fix the rate

nodes.label: Fixed exchange rate regime
nodes.objective: Define a fixed exchange rate as one pegged by the central bank to another currency or basket
essentialPoints: Central bank commits to buying/selling its currency to maintain a set exchange rate
Requires holding foreign exchange reserves to defend the peg

nodes.label: Advantages of a floating exchange rate
nodes.objective: Evaluate the benefits of a floating exchange rate regime
essentialPoints: Automatically adjusts to correct trade imbalances (depreciation boosts exports)
Frees monetary policy to target domestic objectives rather than defending a peg
No need to hold large foreign exchange reserves

nodes.label: Disadvantages of a floating exchange rate
nodes.objective: Evaluate the costs of a floating exchange rate regime
essentialPoints: Exchange rate volatility creates uncertainty for trade and investment
Can be subject to speculative attacks and excessive volatility unrelated to fundamentals
Depreciation can be inflationary via higher import prices

nodes.label: Advantages of a fixed exchange rate
nodes.objective: Evaluate the benefits of a fixed exchange rate regime
essentialPoints: Provides certainty for international trade and investment planning
Can act as a nominal anchor to control domestic inflation
Reduces speculative currency volatility

nodes.label: Disadvantages of a fixed exchange rate
nodes.objective: Evaluate the costs of a fixed exchange rate regime
essentialPoints: Loss of independent monetary policy, as interest rates must defend the peg
Requires large foreign exchange reserves to maintain credibility
Vulnerable to speculative attacks if the peg is seen as unsustainable
Cannot use exchange rate adjustment to correct trade imbalances

nodes.label: Balance of payments: current account and capital/financial account
nodes.objective: Understand the structure of the balance of payments and its component accounts
essentialPoints: Current account records trade in goods/services, income flows, and transfers
Capital/financial account records cross-border asset and investment flows
Overall balance of payments must balance (current account balanced by capital/financial account, subject to reserve changes)

nodes.label: Determinants of net exports
nodes.objective: Understand the factors determining a country's net exports (exports minus imports)
essentialPoints: Net exports depend on the real exchange rate, domestic and foreign income levels
A real depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, raising net exports

nodes.label: Open economy: net exports in the Keynesian cross and the import leakage
nodes.objective: Extend the Keynesian cross/multiplier to an open economy including imports as a leakage
essentialPoints: Imports rise with income, acting as a leakage from the circular flow like saving and taxes
Open economy multiplier is smaller than the closed economy multiplier due to the import leakage

nodes.label: Measuring income inequality: the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient
nodes.objective: Understand the Lorenz curve as a graphical representation of income distribution and the Gini coefficient as a summary measure
essentialPoints: Lorenz curve plots cumulative share of income against cumulative share of population
Perfect equality is the diagonal line; greater bowing away from the diagonal indicates greater inequality
Gini coefficient = area between Lorenz curve and line of equality, divided by total area under the equality line; ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality)

nodes.label: Causes of income inequality
nodes.objective: Identify the main drivers of income inequality within an economy
essentialPoints: Differences in human capital and education driving wage differentials
Technological change favouring skilled over unskilled labour (skill-biased technical change)
Globalisation and trade affecting relative demand for different types of labour
Differences in capital ownership and returns to capital versus labour

nodes.label: Inequality and growth: the equity-efficiency debate
nodes.objective: Evaluate the relationship between inequality and economic growth/efficiency
essentialPoints: Some inequality may be necessary to incentivise effort, innovation, and investment
Excessive inequality can reduce aggregate demand, human capital investment, and social/political stability, harming long-run growth

nodes.label: Policies to reduce inequality: redistribution via taxes and transfers
nodes.objective: Understand how progressive taxation and transfer payments can be used to redistribute income
essentialPoints: Progressive taxation takes a higher proportion of income from higher earners
Transfer payments (welfare benefits) redistribute income towards lower-income households

nodes.label: Evaluating redistribution policy: efficiency costs versus equity gains
nodes.objective: Evaluate the trade-offs involved in using taxes and transfers to reduce inequality
essentialPoints: Redistribution can reduce poverty and social harms associated with high inequality
High marginal tax rates may reduce incentives to work, save, and invest, creating efficiency costs
Administrative and implementation costs of redistribution schemes

nodes.label: Demand: definition and the law of demand
nodes.objective: Understand the relationship between price and quantity demanded, ceteris paribus
essentialPoints: Demand is the quantity of a good buyers are willing/able to buy at each price
Law of demand: quantity demanded falls as price rises, ceteris paribus
Distinguishes movement along the curve from a shift of the curve

nodes.label: Non-price determinants of demand (shifters)
nodes.objective: Identify factors that shift the demand curve
essentialPoints: Income, prices of related goods (substitutes/complements), tastes, expectations, population shift demand
A shift is distinct from a movement along the curve

nodes.label: Constructing a demand curve diagram
nodes.objective: Draw a demand curve with price and quantity axes, showing shifts vs movements
essentialPoints: Price on vertical axis, quantity on horizontal axis
Downward sloping curve represents law of demand
Shifts drawn as parallel/rotated moves of the whole curve

nodes.label: Supply: definition and the law of supply
nodes.objective: Understand relationship between price and quantity supplied
essentialPoints: Supply is quantity sellers are willing/able to sell at each price
Law of supply: quantity supplied rises as price rises, ceteris paribus

nodes.label: Non-price determinants of supply (shifters)
nodes.objective: Identify factors that shift the supply curve
essentialPoints: Input costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of sellers, expectations shift supply
Distinct from movement along the curve

nodes.label: Constructing a supply curve diagram
nodes.objective: Draw a supply curve with price and quantity axes, showing shifts vs movements
essentialPoints: Price on vertical axis, quantity on horizontal axis
Upward sloping curve represents law of supply

nodes.label: Market equilibrium: price and quantity determination
nodes.objective: Find equilibrium as intersection of supply and demand and understand market clearing
essentialPoints: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
At equilibrium price there is no shortage or surplus
Excess demand/supply create pressure toward equilibrium

nodes.label: Comparative statics: shifts and new equilibria
nodes.objective: Analyse how equilibrium price and quantity change following a demand or supply shift
essentialPoints: A shift in one curve moves equilibrium along the other curve
Direction of change in price/quantity depends on which curve shifts and in which direction

nodes.label: Price elasticity of demand: definition and calculation
nodes.objective: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
essentialPoints: PED = %change in quantity demanded / %change in price
Elastic (>1), inelastic (<1), unit elastic (=1) classifications

nodes.label: Determinants of price elasticity of demand
nodes.objective: Identify factors affecting the magnitude of PED
essentialPoints: Availability of substitutes, necessity vs luxury, proportion of income, time horizon

nodes.label: PED and total revenue relationship
nodes.objective: Understand how price changes affect total revenue depending on elasticity
essentialPoints: Price rise increases revenue when demand is inelastic, decreases it when elastic
Revenue maximised at unit elastic point

nodes.label: Income elasticity of demand
nodes.objective: Calculate and interpret income elasticity of demand, classifying normal/inferior goods
essentialPoints: YED = %change in quantity demanded / %change in income
Positive YED implies normal good, negative implies inferior good

nodes.label: Cross-price elasticity of demand
nodes.objective: Calculate and interpret cross-price elasticity, classifying substitutes/complements
essentialPoints: XED = %change in quantity demanded of X / %change in price of Y
Positive XED implies substitutes, negative implies complements

nodes.label: Price elasticity of supply: definition and calculation
nodes.objective: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
essentialPoints: PES = %change in quantity supplied / %change in price
Determined by time horizon, spare capacity, ability to store

nodes.label: Consumer surplus: concept
nodes.objective: Understand consumer surplus as the difference between willingness to pay and price paid
essentialPoints: Consumer surplus = value consumers place on a good minus price actually paid
Aggregated across all units purchased

nodes.label: Producer surplus: concept
nodes.objective: Understand producer surplus as difference between price received and minimum acceptable price
essentialPoints: Producer surplus = price received minus marginal cost of supplying each unit
Aggregated across all units sold

nodes.label: Identifying consumer and producer surplus on a supply-demand diagram
nodes.objective: Shade and calculate consumer and producer surplus areas at equilibrium
essentialPoints: Consumer surplus is the area below demand curve and above price up to equilibrium quantity
Producer surplus is the area above supply curve and below price up to equilibrium quantity

nodes.label: Total surplus and allocative efficiency at market equilibrium
nodes.objective: Understand that unregulated competitive equilibrium maximises total surplus
essentialPoints: Total surplus = consumer surplus + producer surplus
Competitive equilibrium is allocatively efficient absent externalities

nodes.label: Price ceiling (maximum price): definition
nodes.objective: Define a price ceiling as a legal maximum price set below equilibrium
essentialPoints: A price ceiling is a government-imposed maximum legal price
Binding only if set below the equilibrium price

nodes.label: Effects of a binding price ceiling: shortage and welfare loss
nodes.objective: Analyse the shortage and deadweight loss created by a binding price ceiling
essentialPoints: Creates excess demand (shortage) at the capped price
Reduces quantity traded below efficient level, creating deadweight loss
Redistributes surplus from producers to consumers who can obtain the good

nodes.label: Price floor (minimum price): definition
nodes.objective: Define a price floor as a legal minimum price set above equilibrium
essentialPoints: A price floor is a government-imposed minimum legal price
Binding only if set above the equilibrium price

nodes.label: Effects of a binding price floor: surplus and welfare loss
nodes.objective: Analyse the surplus and deadweight loss created by a binding price floor
essentialPoints: Creates excess supply (surplus) at the floor price
Reduces quantity traded below efficient level, creating deadweight loss
Redistributes surplus from consumers to producers who can sell

nodes.label: Tax incidence mechanism: wedge between prices
nodes.objective: Understand how an indirect tax creates a wedge between price paid and price received
essentialPoints: A per-unit tax shifts the supply (or demand) curve by the tax amount
Creates a wedge: buyer price minus seller price equals the tax
New equilibrium quantity is lower than before the tax

nodes.label: Tax incidence and relative elasticities
nodes.objective: Determine how tax burden is split between consumers and producers based on elasticities
essentialPoints: The side of the market with more inelastic response bears more of the tax burden
Relative PED and PES determine incidence split

nodes.label: Deadweight loss from taxation
nodes.objective: Identify and explain the deadweight loss created by an indirect tax
essentialPoints: Tax reduces quantity traded below the efficient level
Deadweight loss is the lost surplus not captured by consumers, producers or government
Size of DWL increases with elasticity of demand and supply

nodes.label: Effects of a subsidy on market equilibrium and welfare
nodes.objective: Analyse how a per-unit subsidy shifts equilibrium and affects welfare
essentialPoints: A subsidy shifts the supply curve outward, lowering the price paid by buyers and raising the price received by sellers
Increases quantity traded above the efficient level, potentially causing deadweight loss when there are no externalities

nodes.label: The rationality assumption in consumer theory
nodes.objective: Understand the assumption that consumers make choices to maximise their own well-being consistently
essentialPoints: Consumers are assumed to have well-defined preferences and choose optimally given constraints
Rationality underlies utility maximisation as a decision framework

nodes.label: Preference axioms: completeness, transitivity, monotonicity
nodes.objective: State and interpret the axioms that make consumer preferences well-behaved
essentialPoints: Completeness: consumer can rank any two bundles
Transitivity: rankings are logically consistent across bundles
Monotonicity (more is better): more of a good is preferred to less

nodes.label: Indifference curves and their properties
nodes.objective: Understand indifference curves as representations of equally preferred bundles
essentialPoints: An indifference curve shows all bundles giving the same utility level
Curves are downward sloping, convex to the origin, and cannot cross
Higher indifference curves represent higher utility

nodes.label: Marginal rate of substitution
nodes.objective: Define MRS as the slope of the indifference curve and the rate of trade-off between goods
essentialPoints: MRS is the rate at which a consumer is willing to trade one good for another while maintaining utility
Equals the negative slope of the indifference curve
Diminishing MRS reflects convex preferences

nodes.label: Utility functions: cardinal vs ordinal representation
nodes.objective: Understand utility as a numerical representation of preferences
essentialPoints: A utility function assigns numbers to bundles consistent with preference ranking
Ordinal utility: only the ranking matters, not magnitude
Cardinal utility: magnitude of differences carries meaning (used in some models)

nodes.label: Marginal utility and diminishing marginal utility
nodes.objective: Define marginal utility and the principle of diminishing marginal utility
essentialPoints: Marginal utility is the additional utility from one more unit of a good
Diminishing marginal utility: MU falls as consumption increases

nodes.label: Common utility function forms (Cobb-Douglas, perfect substitutes, perfect complements)
nodes.objective: Recognise and use standard utility function forms and their indifference curve shapes
essentialPoints: Cobb-Douglas utility gives smooth convex indifference curves
Perfect substitutes give straight-line indifference curves
Perfect complements give L-shaped indifference curves

nodes.label: The budget constraint: definition and equation
nodes.objective: Define the budget constraint as the set of affordable bundles given income and prices
essentialPoints: Budget constraint: total spending cannot exceed income
Equation: p1*x1 + p2*x2 = m defines the budget line
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - budget constraints

nodes.label: Constructing the budget line diagram
nodes.objective: Draw the budget line with correct intercepts and slope
essentialPoints: Intercepts given by income divided by each good's price
Slope equals negative ratio of prices
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - budget constraints

nodes.label: Shifts and rotations of the budget line
nodes.objective: Analyse how changes in income and prices shift or rotate the budget line
essentialPoints: Income change causes parallel shift of the budget line
Price change causes rotation around one intercept
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - budget constraints

nodes.label: Utility maximisation subject to a budget constraint
nodes.objective: Solve for the consumer's optimal bundle where MRS equals the price ratio
essentialPoints: Optimal choice occurs where the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line
Tangency condition: MRS equals the price ratio
Solved formally via constrained optimisation (Lagrangian)

externalPrerequisites.prerequisiteConcept: EC140: constrained optimisation and Lagrangian method

nodes.label: Corner solutions in consumer optimisation
nodes.objective: Recognise when optimal consumption involves zero of one good
essentialPoints: Corner solutions occur with perfect substitutes or non-convex preferences
Tangency condition may not hold; optimum is at a boundary of the budget set

nodes.label: Deriving individual demand curves from utility maximisation
nodes.objective: Derive the demand curve by tracing optimal quantity as price varies
essentialPoints: Varying price of a good and re-solving for optimal quantity traces out the demand curve
Demand curve reflects the price-consumption path

nodes.label: Engel curves and income-consumption path
nodes.objective: Derive the relationship between income and quantity demanded
essentialPoints: Engel curve plots quantity demanded against income at fixed prices
Income-consumption path traces optimal bundles as income varies

nodes.label: Normal and inferior goods
nodes.objective: Classify goods by how demand responds to income changes
essentialPoints: Normal good: demand rises as income rises
Inferior good: demand falls as income rises

nodes.label: The substitution effect of a price change
nodes.objective: Isolate the change in quantity demanded due to a change in relative prices holding utility constant
essentialPoints: Substitution effect holds real income/utility constant and isolates pure relative-price response
Always moves quantity demanded of a good opposite to its own price change
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - substitution/income effects

nodes.label: The income effect of a price change
nodes.objective: Isolate the change in quantity demanded due to the change in real purchasing power from a price change
essentialPoints: Income effect captures the change in real purchasing power caused by the price change
Direction depends on whether the good is normal or inferior
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - substitution/income effects

nodes.label: Slutsky decomposition of a price change
nodes.objective: Decompose the total effect of a price change into substitution and income effects graphically and algebraically
essentialPoints: Total price effect = substitution effect + income effect
Decomposition uses a hypothetical budget line with adjusted income at new prices
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - substitution/income effects

nodes.label: Giffen goods
nodes.objective: Explain how a Giffen good can violate the law of demand
essentialPoints: Giffen good: negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect for a strongly inferior good
Results in quantity demanded rising as price rises, violating law of demand
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - substitution/income effects

nodes.label: Aggregating individual demand into market demand
nodes.objective: Derive market demand by horizontally summing individual demand curves
essentialPoints: Market demand at each price is the sum of quantities demanded by all individuals at that price
Horizontal summation of individual demand curves

nodes.label: Revealed preference: weak axiom (WARP)
nodes.objective: State and apply the weak axiom of revealed preference to test consistency of observed choices
essentialPoints: WARP: if bundle A is chosen when B was affordable, B must never be chosen when A is affordable at different prices/income
Used to infer preferences from observed choices without assuming a utility function
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - revealed preferences

nodes.label: Applying revealed preference to test rationality of choices
nodes.objective: Use observed bundles and prices to check consistency with utility-maximising behaviour
essentialPoints: Compare observed choices across different budget sets to check WARP is not violated
A violation implies choices cannot be rationalised by a stable set of preferences
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - revealed preferences

nodes.label: Bounded rationality and departures from the standard rationality assumption
nodes.objective: Understand that real decision-makers face cognitive limits inconsistent with full rationality
essentialPoints: Bounded rationality: consumers have limited information-processing ability, leading to systematic deviations from the rational choice model
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - behavioural economics

nodes.label: Heuristics and biases in consumer decision-making
nodes.objective: Identify common heuristics and biases that cause deviations from standard rational choice predictions
essentialPoints: Anchoring, framing effects, and present bias distort choices away from utility-maximising predictions
These biases are systematic (not random) departures from the standard model
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - behavioural economics

nodes.label: Prospect theory: loss aversion and reference dependence
nodes.objective: Understand prospect theory as an alternative to expected utility incorporating reference points and loss aversion
essentialPoints: Value is measured relative to a reference point, not absolute wealth
Losses loom larger than equivalent gains (loss aversion)
Value function is concave for gains and convex for losses
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - behavioural economics

nodes.label: Evaluating behavioural economics against the standard rational choice model
nodes.objective: Assess the explanatory power and limitations of behavioural models relative to standard utility maximisation
essentialPoints: Behavioural models explain anomalies (e.g. Giffen-like or loss-averse behaviour) that standard theory struggles with
Standard rational model retains tractability and predictive power for many everyday market outcomes; behavioural models often trade generality/tractability for realism
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Consumer Theory - behavioural economics

nodes.label: The production function: definition
nodes.objective: Define the production function as the relationship between inputs and maximum output
essentialPoints: Production function specifies maximum output obtainable from given quantities of inputs
Typically expressed as a function of capital and labour: Q = f(K,L)

nodes.label: Short run vs long run in production
nodes.objective: Distinguish fixed and variable inputs across time horizons
essentialPoints: Short run: at least one input is fixed
Long run: all inputs are variable

nodes.label: Marginal product of an input
nodes.objective: Define marginal product as the additional output from one more unit of an input
essentialPoints: Marginal product of labour (or capital) is the change in output from one additional unit of that input, holding other inputs fixed

nodes.label: Diminishing marginal returns
nodes.objective: Explain why marginal product eventually declines as more of a variable input is added
essentialPoints: As more of a variable input is added to a fixed input, marginal product eventually decreases
Reflects the fixed factor becoming a binding constraint

nodes.label: Isoquants and their properties
nodes.objective: Understand isoquants as combinations of inputs yielding the same output level
essentialPoints: An isoquant shows all input combinations producing a given output level
Isoquants are downward sloping and convex to the origin (for well-behaved technology)
Higher isoquants represent higher output

nodes.label: Marginal rate of technical substitution
nodes.objective: Define MRTS as the slope of the isoquant and the rate of input substitution
essentialPoints: MRTS is the rate at which one input can be substituted for another while keeping output constant
Equals the ratio of marginal products
Diminishing MRTS reflects convex isoquants

nodes.label: Returns to scale: increasing, constant, decreasing
nodes.objective: Classify production functions by how output responds to proportional changes in all inputs
essentialPoints: Increasing returns to scale: output more than doubles when inputs double
Constant returns to scale: output exactly doubles
Decreasing returns to scale: output less than doubles
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Production - returns to scale

nodes.label: The isocost line
nodes.objective: Define the isocost line as combinations of inputs with equal total cost
essentialPoints: Isocost line: all input combinations costing the same total amount given input prices
Slope equals negative ratio of input prices

nodes.label: Cost minimisation subject to an output target
nodes.objective: Solve for the least-cost combination of inputs producing a given output level
essentialPoints: Optimal input mix occurs where the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line
Tangency condition: MRTS equals the ratio of input prices
Solved via constrained optimisation

externalPrerequisites.prerequisiteConcept: EC140: constrained optimisation and Lagrangian method

nodes.label: Conditional input demand functions
nodes.objective: Derive the cost-minimising quantity of each input as a function of prices and output
essentialPoints: Conditional input demands give cost-minimising input quantities for given input prices and output level
Derived from the cost minimisation tangency condition

nodes.label: The expansion path
nodes.objective: Trace the cost-minimising input combinations as output level varies
essentialPoints: Expansion path connects cost-minimising input bundles across different output levels at fixed input prices

nodes.label: Deriving the total cost function
nodes.objective: Derive total cost as a function of output from the cost minimisation problem
essentialPoints: Total cost function gives minimum cost of producing each output level
Derived by substituting conditional input demands into the cost expression

nodes.label: Fixed cost and variable cost
nodes.objective: Distinguish fixed costs from variable costs in the short run
essentialPoints: Fixed costs do not vary with output level (short run only)
Variable costs change with the level of output

nodes.label: Average fixed, average variable, and average total cost curves
nodes.objective: Derive and interpret AFC, AVC and ATC curves and their typical shapes
essentialPoints: AFC = fixed cost / output, continuously declining
AVC = variable cost / output, typically U-shaped
ATC = AFC + AVC, U-shaped

nodes.label: Marginal cost curve
nodes.objective: Derive marginal cost and its relationship to average cost curves
essentialPoints: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from producing one more unit
MC intersects ATC and AVC at their minimum points

nodes.label: Constructing short-run cost curve diagrams
nodes.objective: Draw AFC, AVC, ATC and MC curves correctly on one diagram
