essentialPoints: Cost on vertical axis, quantity on horizontal axis
MC crosses AVC and ATC at their respective minima

nodes.label: Long-run average cost curve and economies/diseconomies of scale
nodes.objective: Derive the LRAC as the envelope of short-run cost curves and relate its shape to returns to scale
essentialPoints: LRAC is the envelope of all short-run ATC curves at the optimal plant size for each output
Falling LRAC reflects economies of scale, rising LRAC reflects diseconomies of scale
Shape of LRAC relates directly to returns to scale in production
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Production - cost curves, returns to scale

nodes.label: Economic profit: definition
nodes.objective: Define economic profit as total revenue minus total (opportunity) cost
essentialPoints: Economic profit = total revenue minus total economic cost (including opportunity costs)
Differs from accounting profit, which excludes implicit/opportunity costs

nodes.label: Profit maximisation: MR = MC condition
nodes.objective: Derive the general profit-maximising condition applicable to any firm
essentialPoints: Profit is maximised where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
Second-order condition requires MC crossing MR from below

nodes.label: Assumptions of perfect competition
nodes.objective: State the defining assumptions of a perfectly competitive market
essentialPoints: Many buyers and sellers, none able to influence price
Homogeneous product
Free entry and exit
Perfect information

nodes.label: Price-taking behaviour and the firm's demand curve
nodes.objective: Understand why an individual firm faces a perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand curve
essentialPoints: Each firm is too small to affect market price and takes price as given
Firm's individual demand curve is horizontal at the market price

nodes.label: Short-run profit maximisation for a competitive firm
nodes.objective: Apply MR=MC to determine the profit-maximising output for a price-taking firm and identify profit/loss graphically
essentialPoints: Since price equals MR under price-taking, firm produces where P = MC
Profit or loss shown by comparing P to ATC at that output
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Perfect Competition - profit maximisation

nodes.label: Short-run shutdown condition
nodes.objective: Determine when a firm should shut down production in the short run
essentialPoints: Firm shuts down in the short run if price falls below minimum average variable cost
Fixed costs are sunk in the short run and irrelevant to the shutdown decision

nodes.label: Deriving the firm's short-run supply curve
nodes.objective: Derive the competitive firm's supply curve as its marginal cost curve above minimum AVC
essentialPoints: Firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of MC curve above minimum AVC
Below that price, the firm supplies zero (shuts down)

nodes.label: Long-run entry, exit, and zero economic profit
nodes.objective: Explain how free entry and exit drive long-run economic profit to zero
essentialPoints: Positive economic profit attracts entry, shifting market supply out and lowering price
Losses induce exit, shifting supply in and raising price
Long-run equilibrium has price equal to minimum long-run average cost, zero economic profit

nodes.label: Long-run competitive equilibrium: P = MC = min ATC
nodes.objective: State the conditions characterising long-run perfectly competitive equilibrium
essentialPoints: In long-run equilibrium, price equals marginal cost and equals minimum average total cost
Firms are productively efficient, producing at minimum LRAC
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Perfect Competition - market equilibrium

nodes.label: Efficiency of perfect competition: allocative and productive efficiency
nodes.objective: Evaluate perfect competition's welfare properties using consumer and producer surplus
essentialPoints: Perfect competition achieves allocative efficiency (P = MC) and productive efficiency (production at minimum ATC)
Maximises total surplus (consumer plus producer surplus) absent externalities
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Perfect Competition - consumer/producer welfare

nodes.label: Spectrum of market structures and the meaning of market power
nodes.objective: Understand market power as the ability to set price above marginal cost
essentialPoints: Market structures range from perfect competition to monopoly by degree of market power
Market power means a firm's price-setting decision affects market price

nodes.label: Monopoly profit maximisation: MR=MC with downward-sloping demand
nodes.objective: Derive monopoly output and price using the MR=MC rule with a downward-sloping demand curve
essentialPoints: Monopolist faces the entire market (downward-sloping) demand curve
Marginal revenue lies below demand curve since price must fall to sell more units
Monopolist sets output where MR=MC then charges the price the demand curve allows

nodes.label: Monopoly deadweight loss versus perfect competition
nodes.objective: Compare monopoly outcome to competitive outcome and identify the resulting deadweight loss
essentialPoints: Monopoly restricts output and charges a price above marginal cost compared to perfect competition
This creates a deadweight loss and reduces total surplus relative to the competitive outcome

nodes.label: Game theory: the payoff matrix
nodes.objective: Represent a simultaneous game using a payoff matrix of strategies and outcomes
essentialPoints: A payoff matrix lists each player's strategies and the resulting payoffs for every strategy combination
Used to represent simultaneous-move games

nodes.label: Dominant strategy
nodes.objective: Identify a dominant strategy as one that is optimal regardless of the opponent's choice
essentialPoints: A dominant strategy yields the highest payoff for a player no matter what the other player does
Not all games have a dominant strategy for every player

nodes.label: Nash equilibrium
nodes.objective: Define Nash equilibrium as mutual best responses and find it in simple games
essentialPoints: A Nash equilibrium is a strategy profile where no player can improve their payoff by unilaterally deviating
Found via best-response analysis for each player

nodes.label: The prisoner's dilemma
nodes.objective: Analyse the prisoner's dilemma as an example where dominant strategies lead to a suboptimal Nash equilibrium
essentialPoints: Both players have a dominant strategy leading to a worse joint outcome than mutual cooperation
Illustrates the tension between individual and collective rationality

nodes.label: Sequential games and backward induction
nodes.objective: Solve sequential-move games using backward induction to find subgame perfect equilibrium
essentialPoints: Sequential games are represented with a game tree showing order of moves
Backward induction solves from the last decision node backward to find the equilibrium path

nodes.label: Cournot oligopoly model: quantity competition
nodes.objective: Derive Cournot-Nash equilibrium where firms simultaneously choose quantities
essentialPoints: Firms simultaneously choose output quantities, taking rivals' quantities as given
Each firm's best-response function gives its optimal output given the rival's output
Cournot-Nash equilibrium is where all firms' quantities are mutual best responses
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Imperfect Competition & Game Theory - Cournot

nodes.label: Cournot best-response (reaction) functions and equilibrium diagram
nodes.objective: Derive and graph reaction functions to find the Cournot equilibrium quantities
essentialPoints: Each firm's reaction function is derived by maximising its own profit given the rival's quantity
Cournot equilibrium is the intersection of both firms' reaction functions
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Imperfect Competition & Game Theory - Cournot

nodes.label: Stackelberg oligopoly model: sequential quantity leadership
nodes.objective: Solve the Stackelberg model where a leader commits to output before a follower via backward induction
essentialPoints: Leader firm commits to quantity first, follower observes and best-responds
Solved by backward induction: follower's reaction function substituted into leader's profit maximisation
Leader typically produces more and earns higher profit than in Cournot (first-mover advantage)
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Imperfect Competition & Game Theory - Stackelberg

nodes.label: Comparing Cournot and Stackelberg outcomes
nodes.objective: Compare total output, price and profits between Cournot and Stackelberg equilibria
essentialPoints: Stackelberg leader produces more than under Cournot, follower produces less
Total industry output is higher and price lower under Stackelberg than Cournot
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Imperfect Competition & Game Theory

nodes.label: Bertrand oligopoly model: price competition
nodes.objective: Derive the Bertrand equilibrium where firms compete by simultaneously setting prices with homogeneous products
essentialPoints: Firms simultaneously choose prices with homogeneous goods; consumers buy from the lowest-price firm
Bertrand equilibrium (with identical marginal costs) results in price equal to marginal cost, even with only two firms
Known as the Bertrand paradox: competition drives price to marginal cost despite few firms
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Imperfect Competition & Game Theory - Bertrand

nodes.label: Comparing Cournot, Bertrand and Stackelberg predictions
nodes.objective: Evaluate how strategic variable (price vs quantity) and timing (simultaneous vs sequential) affect market outcomes
essentialPoints: Bertrand (price competition) yields the most competitive outcome (P=MC), Cournot (quantity) yields higher prices/profits
Choice of strategic variable and information structure materially changes predicted market outcome, a key limitation of any single oligopoly model
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Imperfect Competition & Game Theory

nodes.label: Collusion and cartel behaviour
nodes.objective: Understand collusive equilibrium as firms jointly restricting output to raise joint profit like a monopolist
essentialPoints: Colluding firms jointly choose output/price to maximise combined profit, mimicking a monopoly outcome
Collusive output is below and price above the Cournot/Bertrand non-cooperative outcome
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Imperfect Competition & Game Theory - collusive equilibria

nodes.label: Incentive to cheat on a collusive agreement
nodes.objective: Explain why an individual firm has an incentive to deviate from a collusive agreement
essentialPoints: Each firm can increase its own short-run profit by secretly producing more than the collusive quantity given the rival holds output fixed
This makes the collusive outcome unstable as a one-shot Nash equilibrium, similar to the prisoner's dilemma
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Imperfect Competition & Game Theory - collusive equilibria

nodes.label: Repeated games and sustaining collusion with trigger strategies
nodes.objective: Explain how repeated interaction and trigger/punishment strategies can sustain collusion over time
essentialPoints: In an infinitely/indefinitely repeated game, threat of future punishment (e.g. reverting to Cournot/Bertrand) can deter cheating
Collusion is more sustainable when firms value future profits highly and detection/punishment is fast
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Imperfect Competition & Game Theory - collusive equilibria

nodes.label: Types of data: categorical, discrete, continuous
nodes.objective: Distinguish categorical, discrete and continuous data.
essentialPoints: Categorical data takes named categories
Discrete data takes countable numeric values
Continuous data can take any value in a range

nodes.label: Frequency distributions and tables
nodes.objective: Construct and read frequency tables for data.
essentialPoints: Frequency counts how often values occur
Relative frequency is frequency divided by total observations
Grouped frequency tables use class intervals for continuous data

nodes.label: Graphical summaries: histograms, bar charts, boxplots
nodes.objective: Construct and interpret histograms, bar charts and boxplots.
essentialPoints: Histograms display frequency distribution of continuous data via bars over intervals
Bar charts display frequency of categorical/discrete data
Boxplots display median, quartiles and range/outliers

nodes.label: Measures of central tendency: mean, median, mode
nodes.objective: Calculate and interpret mean, median and mode.
essentialPoints: Mean is the sum of values divided by number of observations
Median is the middle value of ordered data
Mode is the most frequently occurring value

nodes.label: Measures of dispersion: range, variance, standard deviation, IQR
nodes.objective: Calculate and interpret measures of spread.
essentialPoints: Range is max minus min
Variance is the average squared deviation from the mean
Standard deviation is the square root of variance
Interquartile range is the difference between upper and lower quartiles

nodes.label: Skewness and shape of distributions
nodes.objective: Identify and interpret skewness in a distribution.
essentialPoints: Skewness measures asymmetry of a distribution
Positive skew has a longer right tail; negative skew a longer left tail
Relationship between mean, median position indicates skew direction

nodes.label: Sample spaces, events and probability axioms
nodes.objective: State the axioms of probability and define sample space/events.
essentialPoints: Sample space is the set of all possible outcomes
An event is a subset of the sample space
Probabilities lie between 0 and 1 and sum to 1 over the sample space

nodes.label: Set operations: union, intersection, complement
nodes.objective: Apply set operations to events for probability calculations.
essentialPoints: Union is the probability that at least one of two events occurs
Intersection is the probability both events occur
Complement is the probability an event does not occur

nodes.label: Addition rule of probability
nodes.objective: Apply the addition rule for the probability of a union of events.
essentialPoints: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
Mutually exclusive events have P(A and B) = 0

nodes.label: Conditional probability
nodes.objective: Define and calculate conditional probability.
essentialPoints: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B)
Conditional probability updates likelihood of A given B has occurred

nodes.label: Statistical independence of events
nodes.objective: Determine whether two events are statistically independent.
essentialPoints: Events A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A)
Equivalently P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) for independent events

nodes.label: Multiplication rule of probability
nodes.objective: Apply the multiplication rule to find the probability of joint events.
essentialPoints: P(A and B) = P(A)P(B|A) in general
For independent events this simplifies to P(A)P(B)

nodes.label: Bayes' theorem
nodes.objective: Apply Bayes' theorem to update probabilities given new information.
essentialPoints: Bayes' theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)
Uses the law of total probability to compute P(B)
Allows reversal of a conditional probability

nodes.label: Counting rules: permutations and combinations
nodes.objective: Apply permutation and combination formulas to counting problems.
essentialPoints: Permutations count ordered arrangements
Combinations count unordered selections
Combination formula nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!)

nodes.label: Random variables: definition and notation
nodes.objective: Define a random variable as a function from outcomes to numbers.
essentialPoints: A random variable assigns a numerical value to each outcome in a sample space
Discrete random variables take countable values

nodes.label: Probability mass function
nodes.objective: Define and use the probability mass function of a discrete random variable.
essentialPoints: PMF gives probability that the random variable takes each specific value
Sum of all PMF values equals 1

nodes.label: Cumulative distribution function (discrete case)
nodes.objective: Define and compute the CDF for a discrete random variable.
essentialPoints: CDF gives probability that the random variable is less than or equal to a value
CDF is a non-decreasing step function for discrete variables

nodes.label: Expected value of a discrete random variable
nodes.objective: Calculate the expected value of a discrete random variable.
essentialPoints: Expectation is the probability-weighted average of possible values
E(X) = sum of x times P(X=x)

nodes.label: Variance of a discrete random variable
nodes.objective: Calculate the variance and standard deviation of a discrete random variable.
essentialPoints: Standard deviation is the square root of variance

nodes.label: Algebra of expectation and variance (linear transformations)
nodes.objective: Apply rules for E(aX+b) and Var(aX+b).
essentialPoints: E(aX+b) = aE(X)+b
Var(aX+b) = a^2 Var(X)

nodes.label: Bernoulli trials
nodes.objective: Define a Bernoulli trial and its properties.
essentialPoints: A Bernoulli trial has two outcomes: success or failure
Fixed probability of success p on each trial
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Binomial and Poisson distributions

nodes.label: Binomial distribution: definition, PMF, mean and variance
nodes.objective: Define the binomial distribution and compute its probabilities, mean and variance.
essentialPoints: Binomial distribution models the number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials
PMF: P(X=k) = nCk p^k (1-p)^(n-k)
Mean = np, Variance = np(1-p)
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Binomial and Poisson distributions

nodes.label: Poisson distribution: definition, PMF, mean and variance
nodes.objective: Define the Poisson distribution and compute its probabilities, mean and variance.
essentialPoints: Poisson distribution models the number of events in a fixed interval given a constant average rate
PMF: P(X=k) = e^{-lambda} lambda^k / k!
Mean = Variance = lambda
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Binomial and Poisson distributions

nodes.label: Poisson approximation to the binomial distribution
nodes.objective: Understand and apply the Poisson approximation to the binomial when n is large and p is small.
essentialPoints: When n is large and p is small, binomial can be approximated by Poisson with lambda = np
Simplifies calculation of binomial probabilities in this regime
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Binomial and Poisson distributions

nodes.label: Joint probability distributions (bivariate discrete case)
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation
nodes.objective: Define and use a joint PMF for two discrete random variables.
essentialPoints: Joint PMF gives probability of pairs of outcomes for two random variables
Marginal distributions obtained by summing over the other variable
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation

nodes.label: Marginal and conditional distributions
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation
nodes.objective: Derive marginal and conditional distributions from a joint distribution.
essentialPoints: Marginal distribution of X sums the joint distribution over all values of Y
Conditional distribution of X given Y=y is the joint PMF divided by the marginal of Y
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation

nodes.label: Covariance between two random variables
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation
nodes.objective: Define and calculate covariance between two random variables.
essentialPoints: Cov(X,Y) = E[(X-E(X))(Y-E(Y))] = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y)
Covariance measures the direction of linear association between two variables
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation

nodes.label: Correlation coefficient
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation
nodes.objective: Define and interpret the correlation coefficient.
essentialPoints: Correlation standardises covariance by the product of standard deviations
Correlation coefficient lies between -1 and 1
Correlation measures strength and direction of linear relationship
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation

nodes.label: Independence and covariance/correlation of independent variables
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation
nodes.objective: Understand the relationship between independence and covariance/correlation.
essentialPoints: Independent random variables have zero covariance
Zero covariance does not imply independence
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation

nodes.label: Mean and variance of sums of random variables
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation
nodes.objective: Derive the mean and variance of a linear combination of random variables.
essentialPoints: E(X+Y) = E(X)+E(Y) always
Var(X+Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)
Var(X+Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y) if X and Y independent
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Bivariate distributions; covariance and correlation

nodes.label: Continuous random variables and probability density functions
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions
nodes.objective: Define a continuous random variable and its probability density function.
essentialPoints: Continuous random variables take any value in an interval
PDF is a function whose area under the curve gives probability
Probability of any exact single value is zero for continuous variables
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions

nodes.label: Cumulative distribution function (continuous case)
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions
nodes.objective: Define and use the CDF of a continuous random variable, its relation to the PDF via integration.
essentialPoints: CDF is the integral of the PDF up to a value
PDF is the derivative of the CDF
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions

nodes.label: Expectation and variance for continuous random variables
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions
nodes.objective: Calculate expectation and variance for continuous random variables using integration.
essentialPoints: E(X) is the integral of x times the PDF over its support
Variance formula analogous to discrete case using integration
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions

nodes.label: Uniform distribution
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions
nodes.objective: Define the uniform distribution and compute probabilities, mean and variance.
essentialPoints: Uniform distribution has constant density over an interval [a,b]
Mean = (a+b)/2, Variance = (b-a)^2/12
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions

nodes.label: Normal distribution: definition and properties
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions
nodes.objective: Define the normal distribution and describe its key properties.
essentialPoints: Normal distribution is a symmetric bell-shaped continuous distribution defined by mean and variance
PDF given by the normal density formula
Approximately 68/95/99.7% of values lie within 1/2/3 standard deviations
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions

nodes.label: Standard normal distribution and z-scores
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions
nodes.objective: Standardise a normal random variable and use z-tables.
essentialPoints: Standard normal has mean 0 and variance 1
Z = (X - mean)/standard deviation converts any normal variable to standard normal
Standard normal tables/CDF used to find probabilities
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions

nodes.label: Normal approximation to the binomial distribution
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions
nodes.objective: Apply the normal approximation to binomial probabilities including continuity correction.
essentialPoints: For large n, binomial can be approximated by normal with mean np and variance np(1-p)
Continuity correction adjusts for approximating discrete by continuous distribution
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Continuous random variables; uniform and normal distributions

nodes.label: Law of large numbers
nodes.objective: State and interpret the law of large numbers.
essentialPoints: As sample size increases, the sample mean converges to the population mean
Justifies using sample averages to estimate population parameters

nodes.label: Central limit theorem
nodes.objective: State and apply the central limit theorem.
essentialPoints: The distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows, regardless of the population distribution
Sample mean has mean mu and variance sigma^2/n

nodes.label: Population, sample and random sampling
nodes.objective: Distinguish population from sample and define simple random sampling.
essentialPoints: Population is the entire group of interest; sample is a subset drawn from it
Random sampling gives every member of the population a known chance of selection
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Sampling and sampling distributions

nodes.label: Sample statistics: sample mean and sample variance as estimators
nodes.objective: Define sample mean and sample variance as random variables computed from a sample.
essentialPoints: Sample mean is the average of observed sample values
Sample variance estimates population variance using (n-1) in the denominator
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Sampling and sampling distributions

nodes.label: Sampling distribution of the sample mean
nodes.objective: Describe the sampling distribution of the sample mean and its parameters.
essentialPoints: Sampling distribution describes how the sample mean varies across repeated samples
Its mean equals the population mean and its standard deviation is the standard error
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Sampling and sampling distributions

nodes.label: Standard error of the mean
nodes.objective: Define and calculate the standard error of the sample mean.
essentialPoints: Standard error = population standard deviation divided by square root of sample size
Standard error decreases as sample size increases
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Sampling and sampling distributions

nodes.label: Student's t-distribution
nodes.objective: Describe the t-distribution and when it replaces the normal distribution.
essentialPoints: t-distribution used when population variance is unknown and estimated from the sample
t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal and depends on degrees of freedom
As sample size increases, t-distribution approaches the normal distribution
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Sampling and sampling distributions

nodes.label: Point estimation and desirable estimator properties
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Understand point estimators and properties such as unbiasedness and efficiency.
essentialPoints: A point estimator produces a single value estimate of a population parameter
Unbiasedness means the expected value of the estimator equals the true parameter
Efficiency compares estimators by their variance
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Confidence intervals for a population mean
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Construct and interpret confidence intervals for a population mean.
essentialPoints: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter with a stated confidence level
CI = sample mean plus/minus critical value times standard error
Uses z-distribution when variance known, t-distribution when unknown
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Null and alternative hypotheses
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Formulate null and alternative hypotheses for a testing problem.
essentialPoints: Null hypothesis represents the default/no-effect claim to be tested
Alternative hypothesis represents the claim of interest if the null is rejected
Tests can be one-tailed or two-tailed depending on the alternative
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Test statistics and significance level
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Compute a test statistic and compare to a significance level to reach a decision.
essentialPoints: Test statistic standardises the sample evidence relative to the null hypothesis
Significance level (alpha) is the threshold probability for rejecting the null
Decision made by comparing test statistic to critical value or p-value to alpha
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: P-values
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Define and interpret a p-value in hypothesis testing.
essentialPoints: P-value is the probability of observing a test statistic as extreme as the sample result, assuming the null is true
Small p-value provides evidence against the null hypothesis
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Type I and Type II errors
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Distinguish Type I and Type II errors and their relationship to significance and power.
essentialPoints: Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis, with probability alpha
Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis, with probability beta
Power of a test is 1 minus beta
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Hypothesis testing for a population mean
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Carry out a hypothesis test for a single population mean.
essentialPoints: Uses sample mean and standard error to construct a z or t test statistic against the hypothesised mean
Decision rule compares test statistic/p-value to significance level
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Hypothesis testing for the difference between two means
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Carry out a hypothesis test comparing two population means.
essentialPoints: Test statistic uses the difference in sample means and combined standard error
Assumptions differ for independent vs paired samples and equal vs unequal variances
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals for a proportion
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Construct confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for a population proportion.
essentialPoints: Sample proportion approximated as normally distributed for large samples
Standard error of a proportion uses p(1-p)/n
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Chi-squared distribution
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Describe the chi-squared distribution and its role in testing.
essentialPoints: Chi-squared distribution arises from sums of squared standard normal variables
Shape depends on degrees of freedom and is right-skewed
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Chi-squared test of goodness of fit / independence
nodes.subtopic: EC124 - Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
nodes.objective: Carry out a chi-squared test for goodness of fit or independence in a contingency table.
essentialPoints: Test statistic compares observed and expected frequencies
Used to test whether a distribution fits a hypothesised form or whether two categorical variables are independent
specRefs: EC124 syllabus: Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals

nodes.label: Rationale for non-parametric methods
nodes.objective: Explain when non-parametric tests are preferred over parametric tests.
essentialPoints: Non-parametric tests do not assume a specific population distribution (e.g. normality)
Useful for ordinal data or small samples where distributional assumptions are doubtful

nodes.label: Sign test
nodes.objective: Carry out the sign test for a median or paired comparison.
essentialPoints: Sign test uses only the sign of the difference from a hypothesised median or between paired observations
Test statistic follows a binomial distribution under the null

nodes.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
nodes.objective: Carry out the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired data.
essentialPoints: Ranks the absolute differences between paired observations and sums ranks by sign
Tests whether the median difference is zero, more powerful than the sign test when data are symmetric

nodes.label: Mann-Whitney U test
nodes.objective: Carry out the Mann-Whitney U test to compare two independent samples.
essentialPoints: Ranks all observations from both samples combined and compares rank sums
Tests whether two independent samples come from the same distribution without assuming normality

nodes.label: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient
nodes.objective: Calculate and interpret Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.
essentialPoints: Measures the strength and direction of a monotonic relationship using ranked data
Alternative to Pearson correlation when data are ordinal or non-linear

nodes.label: Recap: single-variable differentiation rules
nodes.subtopic: EC140 - Calculus of functions of two or more variables
nodes.objective: Recall standard differentiation rules (power, product, quotient, chain) as a foundation for multivariable calculus.
essentialPoints: Power, product, quotient and chain rules
Differentiation of exponential and logarithmic functions
These rules extend directly to partial differentiation
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Calculus of functions of two or more variables

nodes.label: Functions of two or more variables
nodes.subtopic: EC140 - Calculus of functions of two or more variables
nodes.objective: Understand notation and interpretation of multivariable functions such as z = f(x,y).
essentialPoints: A function can map several independent variables to one output
Graphical interpretation as a surface in 3D
Economic examples: utility function u(x,y), production function q(K,L)
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Calculus of functions of two or more variables

nodes.label: Partial derivatives (first order)
nodes.subtopic: EC140 - Calculus of functions of two or more variables
nodes.objective: Compute first-order partial derivatives of multivariable functions holding other variables constant.
essentialPoints: Differentiate with respect to one variable holding others fixed
Notation: ∂f/∂x, f_x
Interpreted as marginal effect, e.g. marginal utility, marginal product
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Calculus of functions of two or more variables

nodes.label: Second-order and cross partial derivatives
nodes.subtopic: EC140 - Calculus of functions of two or more variables
nodes.objective: Compute second-order own partials and cross partials, and apply Young's theorem.
essentialPoints: f_xx, f_yy measure curvature in each direction
f_xy = f_yx (Young's theorem) under continuity
Used to check concavity/convexity and diminishing marginal returns
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Calculus of functions of two or more variables

nodes.label: Total differential
nodes.subtopic: EC140 - Calculus of functions of two or more variables
nodes.objective: Construct the total differential of a multivariable function as the sum of partial effects.
essentialPoints: dz = f_x dx + f_y dy
Approximates the total change in z from small changes in all variables
Building block for comparative statics and implicit differentiation
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Calculus of functions of two or more variables

nodes.label: Chain rule for multivariable functions
nodes.subtopic: EC140 - Calculus of functions of two or more variables
nodes.objective: Differentiate composite multivariable functions where variables themselves depend on other variables.
essentialPoints: dz/dt = f_x (dx/dt) + f_y (dy/dt) when x,y depend on t
Extends single-variable chain rule to several intermediate variables
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Calculus of functions of two or more variables

nodes.label: Implicit differentiation and implicit function theorem
nodes.subtopic: EC140 - Calculus of functions of two or more variables
nodes.objective: Differentiate implicitly defined relationships F(x,y)=c to find dy/dx without solving explicitly for y.
essentialPoints: dy/dx = -F_x/F_y along a level curve F(x,y)=c
Implicit function theorem gives conditions for this slope to exist
Used to derive slopes of indifference curves and isoquants
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Calculus of functions of two or more variables

nodes.label: Level curves and their slope
nodes.subtopic: EC140 - Calculus of functions of two or more variables
nodes.objective: Interpret a level curve of a multivariable function and relate its slope to the marginal rate of substitution/technical substitution.
essentialPoints: A level curve holds f(x,y) equal to a constant
Its slope equals -f_x/f_y (via implicit differentiation)
Economic interpretation: MRS along an indifference curve, MRTS along an isoquant
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Calculus of functions of two or more variables

nodes.label: Homogeneous functions and Euler's theorem
nodes.subtopic: EC140 - Calculus of functions of two or more variables
nodes.objective: Define degree of homogeneity and apply Euler's theorem relating a function to its partial derivatives.
essentialPoints: f(tx,ty) = t^k f(x,y) defines degree-k homogeneity
Euler's theorem: x f_x + y f_y = k f(x,y)
Used to characterise returns to scale in production functions
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Calculus of functions of two or more variables

nodes.label: Unconstrained optimisation: first and second order conditions (one variable)
nodes.objective: Find and classify stationary points of a single-variable function using first and second derivatives.
essentialPoints: FOC: f'(x)=0 identifies stationary points
SOC: f''(x)<0 for max, f''(x)>0 for min
Distinguishes maxima, minima, and inflection points
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Unconstrained optimisation of multivariable functions (FOC)
nodes.objective: Find candidate stationary points of a multivariable function by setting all first partial derivatives to zero.
essentialPoints: FOCs: f_x=0 and f_y=0 simultaneously
Solving the system gives candidate optimum points
Necessary but not sufficient condition for an optimum
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Second-order conditions via the Hessian (bordered-free case)
nodes.objective: Use the Hessian matrix of second partials to classify stationary points as maxima, minima, or saddle points.
essentialPoints: Hessian collects f_xx, f_yy, f_xy
Sign conditions on determinant and leading principal minors classify the stationary point
Saddle points arise when conditions are mixed
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Concavity and convexity of functions
nodes.objective: Determine whether a function is concave or convex using second derivative/Hessian conditions and relate this to global optima.
essentialPoints: Concave function: second derivative/Hessian negative semi-definite
Convex function: positive semi-definite
Concavity guarantees a stationary point is a global maximum
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Lagrange multiplier method for equality-constrained optimisation
nodes.objective: Set up and solve a constrained optimisation problem using the Lagrangian function.
essentialPoints: Form L = f(x,y) + λ(c - g(x,y))
Solves the system to find the constrained optimum
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Interpretation of the Lagrange multiplier (shadow price)
nodes.objective: Interpret λ as the marginal value of relaxing the constraint.
essentialPoints: λ measures the change in the optimal objective value per unit relaxation of the constraint
Economic interpretation as a shadow price, e.g. marginal utility of income
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Second-order conditions for constrained optimisation (bordered Hessian)
nodes.objective: Use the bordered Hessian to verify that a Lagrangian stationary point is a genuine constrained maximum or minimum.
essentialPoints: Bordered Hessian augments the Hessian with constraint gradients
Sign pattern of bordered leading principal minors classifies constrained max/min
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Optimisation with inequality constraints (Kuhn-Tucker conditions)
nodes.objective: Extend Lagrangian optimisation to inequality constraints using complementary slackness conditions.
essentialPoints: Constraint g(x,y)≤c may or may not bind at the optimum
Complementary slackness: λ≥0 and λ(c-g(x,y))=0
Used for corner solutions, e.g. non-negativity constraints in consumer choice
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Application: constrained utility maximisation subject to a budget constraint
nodes.objective: Apply the Lagrangian method to derive optimal consumer choice given a budget constraint.
essentialPoints: Maximise u(x,y) subject to px x + py y = m
Tangency condition MRS = price ratio derived from FOCs
Solution gives Marshallian demand functions
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Application: constrained cost minimisation subject to an output constraint
nodes.objective: Apply the Lagrangian method to derive a firm's cost-minimising input choice given an output target.
essentialPoints: Minimise wL + rK subject to q(K,L)=q0
Tangency condition MRTS = input price ratio derived from FOCs
Solution gives conditional factor demands
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Unconstrained and constrained optimisation

nodes.label: Comparative statics: concept and purpose
nodes.objective: Understand comparative statics as analysing how an equilibrium/optimum changes when an exogenous parameter changes.
essentialPoints: Compares two equilibria before and after a parameter shift
Distinguishes exogenous parameters from endogenous (choice/equilibrium) variables
Foundational tool for signing effects of policy or preference changes

nodes.label: Comparative statics via implicit differentiation of FOCs
nodes.objective: Differentiate an equilibrium condition implicitly with respect to a parameter to sign the response of the endogenous variable.
essentialPoints: Totally differentiate the FOC/equilibrium condition with respect to the parameter
Solve for dx*/dα using implicit differentiation
Sign of the result depends on sign of numerator/denominator terms

nodes.label: Application: comparative statics of market equilibrium
nodes.objective: Apply comparative statics to determine how equilibrium price and quantity respond to shifts in demand or supply parameters.
essentialPoints: Set demand=supply as an equilibrium condition in terms of parameters
Differentiate implicitly to find dP*/dα, dQ*/dα
Signs match textbook demand/supply shift predictions

nodes.label: Comparative statics of constrained optimisation solutions
nodes.objective: Analyse how the solution to a Lagrangian problem changes as a parameter (e.g. income, price) changes.
essentialPoints: Differentiate the FOC system from the Lagrangian with respect to the parameter
Use Cramer's rule with the bordered Hessian to solve for comparative static derivatives
Produces results such as the effect of income on optimal demand

nodes.label: Matrices and vectors: definitions and notation
nodes.objective: Define a matrix, vector, and their dimensions and notation.
essentialPoints: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers with rows and columns
A vector is a matrix with one row or one column
Notation: element a_ij denotes row i, column j

nodes.label: Matrix addition, scalar multiplication, and multiplication
nodes.objective: Perform addition, scalar multiplication and matrix multiplication, respecting conformability rules.
essentialPoints: Addition requires matching dimensions, done element-wise
Scalar multiplication multiplies every element
Matrix multiplication requires inner dimensions to match; not commutative in general

nodes.label: Matrix transpose
nodes.objective: Compute the transpose of a matrix and know its basic properties.
essentialPoints: Transpose swaps rows and columns
(AB)^T = B^T A^T
Symmetric matrix satisfies A = A^T

nodes.label: Determinants of matrices
nodes.objective: Compute determinants of 2x2 and 3x3 matrices and interpret their sign/magnitude.
essentialPoints: 2x2 determinant: ad-bc
3x3 via cofactor expansion
A zero determinant indicates a singular (non-invertible) matrix

nodes.label: Matrix inverse
nodes.objective: Compute the inverse of a matrix using the adjugate/determinant method and know when it exists.
essentialPoints: A^{-1} exists only if det(A)≠0
A^{-1} = adj(A)/det(A)

nodes.label: Representing systems of linear equations in matrix form
nodes.objective: Write a system of linear equations as Ax=b.
essentialPoints: Coefficient matrix A, variable vector x, constant vector b
Solvability relates to whether A is invertible

nodes.label: Solving linear systems using matrix inversion and Cramer's rule
nodes.objective: Solve Ax=b using x=A^{-1}b or Cramer's rule with determinants.
essentialPoints: x = A^{-1}b when A is invertible
Cramer's rule replaces columns of A with b and takes ratios of determinants
Used to solve simultaneous equilibrium/FOC systems

nodes.label: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
nodes.objective: Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix and relate them to definiteness and dynamic stability.
essentialPoints: Eigenvalues solve det(A-λI)=0
Eigenvectors satisfy (A-λI)v=0
Signs of eigenvalues used to classify definiteness of Hessians and stability of dynamic systems

nodes.label: Application: matrix algebra in solving linear economic models
nodes.objective: Set up and solve a simple multi-market or IS-LM-style linear economic model using matrix methods.
essentialPoints: Express simultaneous equilibrium conditions as a linear system
Solve via matrix inversion or Cramer's rule for equilibrium values
Interpret comparative statics results from the solved system

nodes.label: Simple interest
nodes.objective: Calculate simple interest and future value under simple interest.
essentialPoints: Interest is calculated only on the principal each period
FV = P(1+rt)

nodes.label: Compound interest
nodes.objective: Calculate compound interest and future value under compounding, including varying compounding frequency.
essentialPoints: FV = P(1+r/n)^{nt} for n compounding periods per year
Interest earns interest, compounding accelerates growth
More frequent compounding raises the effective annual rate

nodes.label: Continuous compounding and the exponential function
nodes.objective: Derive and use the continuous compounding formula as the limit of discrete compounding.
essentialPoints: FV = Pe^{rt} as n→∞ in the compound interest formula
Links financial mathematics to properties of the exponential function

nodes.label: Present value and discounting
nodes.objective: Calculate the present value of a single future cash flow given a discount rate.
essentialPoints: PV = FV/(1+r)^t
Discounting reflects time preference and opportunity cost of money
Inverse operation to compounding

nodes.label: Geometric series and their sum formula
nodes.objective: Recall the geometric series sum formula, including the infinite sum case, as a tool for valuing cash flow streams.
essentialPoints: Finite sum: a(1-r^n)/(1-r)
Infinite sum (|r|<1): a/(1-r)
Prerequisite algebraic tool for annuity/perpetuity valuation

nodes.label: Valuing annuities
nodes.objective: Derive and apply the present value formula for a finite stream of equal cash flows.
essentialPoints: PV of an annuity = C[1-(1+r)^{-n}]/r derived from the geometric series formula
Used to value loans, mortgages, and regular payment streams

nodes.label: Valuing perpetuities
nodes.objective: Derive and apply the present value formula for an infinite stream of equal cash flows.
essentialPoints: PV of a perpetuity = C/r, from the infinite geometric series limit
Used to value assets with indefinite constant payments (e.g. consols)

nodes.label: Net present value and internal rate of return
nodes.objective: Calculate NPV of a project's cash flows and define IRR as the discount rate setting NPV to zero.
essentialPoints: NPV = sum of discounted cash flows minus initial cost
Accept a project if NPV>0
IRR solves NPV(r)=0; used as an alternative investment appraisal criterion

nodes.label: Sequences: definition and notation
nodes.objective: Understand a sequence as an ordered list of terms indexed by discrete time.
essentialPoints: Sequence x_t defined for integer time periods t=0,1,2,...
Can be defined explicitly or recursively
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Introduction to difference equations

nodes.label: First-order linear difference equations: solution method
nodes.objective: Solve a first-order linear difference equation x_{t+1}=ax_t+b for the general and particular solution.
essentialPoints: General form x_{t+1} = a x_t + b
Solution combines a homogeneous term a^t and a particular (steady-state) solution
Particular solution found by setting x_{t+1}=x_t=x* at steady state
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Introduction to difference equations

nodes.label: Stability and convergence of difference equation solutions
nodes.objective: Determine whether the solution path of a first-order difference equation converges to, oscillates around, or diverges from the steady state.
essentialPoints: Convergence/divergence determined by the coefficient a: |a|<1 converges, |a|>1 diverges
a<0 produces oscillation, a>0 monotonic approach
Long-run behaviour is the steady state x* when the system is stable
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Introduction to difference equations

nodes.label: Application: difference equations in dynamic economic models
nodes.objective: Apply first-order difference equation methods to a simple dynamic economic model such as the cobweb model or capital accumulation.
essentialPoints: Set up a period-to-period economic relationship as a difference equation
Solve for the time path and steady state
Interpret stability conditions economically (e.g. cobweb convergence depends on relative slopes of supply and demand)
specRefs: EC140 syllabus: Introduction to difference equations

nodes.label: Mathematical computing skills (statistical/mathematical software)
nodes.objective: Use statistical/mathematical software to graph functions and implement the mathematical methods covered in the module.
essentialPoints: Plot functions of one and two variables using software
Perform matrix operations and solve equations computationally
Use software to verify optimisation and comparative statics results numerically
